facts.text: Code verification checks that simulation software has no errors in how it solves its equations; solution verification estimates the numerical error remaining in a particular run.
facts.quote: Code verification checks that the simulation software has no errors in how it solves its equations; solution verification estimates how much numerical error remains in one particular run.

facts.text: Code verification tests simulation software against problems with known exact answers to catch programming mistakes and is performed once per software version.
facts.quote: Code verification tests the program against problems with known exact answers to catch programming mistakes; it is done once per software version.

facts.text: Solution verification is performed for each kind of simulation run by shortening the time step or refining the spatial grid and checking whether the answer settles.
facts.quote: Solution verification is done for each kind of run: the engineer shortens the time step or refines the grid and watches whether the answer settles.

facts.text: If halving a simulation time step changes stopping distance from 41.9 m to 41.2 m, the numerical error is of that order and must be included in the uncertainty budget.
facts.quote: If a stopping distance moves from 41.9 m to 41.2 m when the time step is halved, the numerical error is of that order and belongs in the uncertainty budget.

facts.text: The space agency standard lists “implementation and solution verification” as a simulation credibility factor.
facts.quote: The space agency standard lists "implementation and solution verification" as a credibility factor

facts.text: The shared structure of all the simulation credibility frameworks places code and solution verification before any comparison with physical data.
facts.quote: the shared structure of all the frameworks places "verify code and solution" before any comparison with physical data [Chapter 10].

facts.text: A simulation model cannot be validated honestly until its numerical errors are known, because a numerical artifact may be mistaken for physics or tuned away.
facts.quote: Until its numerical errors are known, a model cannot be validated honestly, because a numerical artifact may be mistaken for physics or tuned away.

facts.text: The booklet's assessor checklist asks for verification evidence that simulation equations were implemented and solved correctly rather than correlated after tuning.
facts.quote: The booklet's assessor checklist asks for verification evidence showing that the equations were "implemented and solved correctly rather than correlated after tuning" [Chapter 10].
